newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Shell seeks to double Africa business by 2002.
newsitem.headline: Shell seeks to double Africa business by 2002.

text.p: Royal Dutch/Shell plans to double its business in sub-Saharan Africa over the next five years, group mananging director Phil Watts said in an interview.
Watts told Reuters in South Africa during a familiarisation visit this week that the group had a wide range of plans to boost productivity and sales in Africa.
He said the group could realistically expect to double its sales, its wealth creation and its tax contribution on the sub-continent.
"There are all kinds of measures of growth -- value, productivity, capital employed," Watts said.
"What's absolutely clear is that we plan to be twice the size that we are now within the next five years in terms of total intergrated business in Africa below the Sahara."
Watts, who has overall responsibility for exploration and research in Africa, visited South Africa en route to Harare to address an African/African-American summit on Thursday.
He said in the interview, given on Tuesday for release on Thursday, that Shell marketed oil products in 30 African countries and provided 10 percent of the continent's oil needs.
The group had an interest in six African refineries, including the continent's largest in Durban, South Africa.
"Our market share in most places is going up. Maybe that's because some people are losing heart about business in Africa and we're not," he said.
Projects already approved or under consideration include:
- Expanding the petrol production capacity of the South African refinery by about 20 percent.
- Producing natural gas from the Kudu field off Namibia for electricity generation there and pipeline supply to the Western Cape region around Cape Town.
- Construction of a four billion dollar liquified natural gas plant in Nigeria to facilitate gas exports and cut the flaring associated with the Nigerian oil operation.
- Development in an Exxon-operated consortium of oilfields in Chad, possibly including a 1,000 km (660 mile) pipeline across Cameroon.
- Deep-water exploration off the Ivory Coast, Nigeria, Gabon, the two Congos and Angola.
- Development and marketing of low-cost energy technology for domestic use in rural areas.
"Development is the key challenge for the people of this continent. Supporting this development is a major challenge for the world community," Watts told the Harare summit.

"Widespread political changes have brought new attitudes to economic development and to the role of external investors. This is vital for attracting the capital flows and associated transfer of skills that have been so important for progress elsewhere."
Sustainable African development would have to combine economic and human development with environmental sustainability, he said.

"Multinational investors can play a vital role in pursuing all three pillars of sustainable development, (but) they can only do so through long-term partnerships with African peoples and their governments."
